summary: This memo gives an overview of version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, called SNMPv2. This early version of SNMPv2 is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Version 2 of SNMP was not written as one document but as a set of them, one for each part of the design. This memo is the map: it says which document defines which part.

questions: which document defines the smi for snmpv2
how does snmpv2 map onto udp
subtitle: Overview of version 2 of the Internet-standard framework for managing networks, and where each part is defined.

tldr.problem: SNMPv1 was spread across three separate documents, and network managers needed an overview of what version 2 of the framework contained and which document defined each part.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1441 walks through the components of SNMPv2: the Structure of Management Information, textual conventions, protocol operations, transport mappings, protocol instrumentation, the administrative framework and conformance statements, naming the separate document that defines each one.
tldr.outcome: The memo is an introduction, not a specification. It is a Historic RFC from April 1993, and its security section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

today: RFC 1441 is a Historic RFC from April 1993. It is an introduction to version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework rather than a specification, and each part of that framework is defined in a separate document. Its security considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: An Overview, Not a Specification
sections.content:
RFC 1441 defines no protocol. It is an introduction to version 2 of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, called SNMPv2, and it points to the document that defines each part of that framework.

SNMPv2 is derived from the original Internet-standard Network Management Framework, SNMPv1, which consists of three documents. RFC 1155 defines the Structure of Management Information (SMI), the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. RFC 1212 defines a more concise description mechanism, which is wholly consistent with the SMI. RFC 1157 defines the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) itself, the protocol used for network access to managed objects.

Version 2 keeps that division of labour and adds more parts. This memo names ten of them, together with the document that defines each: the SMI, textual conventions, conformance statements, the administrative model, the security protocols, the Party MIB, the protocol operations, the transport mappings, the Management Information Base for SNMPv2, and the Manager-to-Manager MIB. The memo also records that the framework builds on the technical direction set by the original authors of the SGMP, which was invented in 1987.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a guide to a set of documents, not a protocol itself. It lists the parts of the second version of SNMP and names the document that defines each part.

sections.title: The Parts of a Network Management System
sections.content:
A network management system contains several, possibly many, nodes. Each node has a processing entity called an agent, which has access to management instrumentation. There is at least one management station, and there is a management protocol used to convey management information between the agents and the management stations. Operations of the protocol are carried out under an administrative framework, which defines both authentication and authorization policies.

Management stations execute management applications, which monitor and control network elements. Network elements are devices such as hosts, routers and terminal servers, and they are monitored and controlled through access to their management information.
sections.plainLanguage: Every managed device runs a small program that answers questions about it. A management station sends those questions over the network and collects the answers. An administrative framework decides who may ask what.

sections.title: The Structure of Management Information
sections.content:
Management information is a collection of managed objects residing in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB). Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules, and these modules are written using a subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1). The SMI is divided into three parts. Module definitions describe information modules, and the ASN.1 macro MODULE-IDENTITY conveys the semantics of such a module. Object definitions describe managed objects, and OBJECT-TYPE conveys the syntax and semantics of a managed object. The third part, trap definitions, also called notification definitions, describe unsolicited transmissions of management information, and NOTIFICATION-TYPE conveys the syntax and semantics of a notification.

When a MIB module needs a type that the SMI does not define, the module can define a textual convention: a new type with a different name, a syntax similar to a type defined in the SMI, and a more precise semantics. Objects defined using a textual convention are always encoded by the rules that define their primitive type, although a convention often has special semantics attached to it. The macro TEXTUAL-CONVENTION conveys the syntax and semantics of the convention, and the Textual Conventions document defines the initial set of textual conventions available to all MIB modules.
sections.plainLanguage: All the facts a device reports are organised into named objects and written down in a standard notation called ASN.1. A module can also give a common type a more precise name, so a reader knows exactly what it means.

sections.title: Protocol Operations and Transport Mappings
sections.content:
The management protocol provides for the exchange of messages that convey management information between the agents and the management stations. The form of each message is a wrapper that encapsulates a Protocol Data Unit (PDU). The form and the meaning of that wrapper are determined by an administrative framework, which defines both authentication and authorization policies. The Protocol Operations document defines the operations of the protocol with respect to the sending and receiving of the PDUs.

SNMPv2 may be used over a variety of protocol suites. The Transport Mappings document defines how SNMPv2 maps onto an initial set of transport domains, and other mappings may be defined in the future. Although several mappings are defined, the mapping onto UDP is the preferred one. To provide the greatest level of interoperability, systems that deploy other mappings should also provide for proxy service to the UDP mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: A management request travels inside a wrapper that says who is sending it and what they may do. The wrapper holds the request itself. UDP is the preferred way to carry these messages over the network.

sections.title: The Administrative Framework
sections.content:
An SNMPv2 party is a conceptual, virtual execution context whose operation is restricted, for security or other purposes, to an administratively defined subset of all possible operations of a particular SNMPv2 entity. Associated with each party is a single authentication protocol and a single privacy protocol.

The administrative model document defines the behaviour of an SNMPv2 party. The security protocols document defines the authentication and privacy protocols used by parties. The Party MIB defines managed objects which correspond to the properties associated with an SNMPv2 party.
sections.plainLanguage: Each manager acts as a party, and each party has its own rules about what it may look at and change. A request outside those rules is refused.

sections.title: Conformance Statements and Instrumentation
sections.content:
It may be useful to define the acceptable lower bounds of an implementation, along with the actual level of implementation achieved. The Conformance Statements document defines the notation used for this, in two kinds. Compliance statements describe requirements for agents with respect to object definitions, and the ASN.1 macro MODULE-COMPLIANCE conveys such requirements. Capability statements describe the capabilities of agents with respect to object definitions, and the macro AGENT-CAPABILITIES conveys them. Collections of related objects are grouped together to form a unit of conformance, and the macro OBJECT-GROUP conveys the syntax and semantics of such a group.

Two MIB documents describe behaviour. The Management Information Base for SNMPv2 defines managed objects which describe the behaviour of an SNMPv2 entity, and the Manager-to-Manager MIB defines an initial set of managed objects which describe the behaviour of an SNMPv2 entity acting in a manager role. The memo expects extensions to that MIB to be defined in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Vendors agree on what a device must support and what it may support. That way two devices from different makers can be managed by the same program.

viz.caption: THE ASN.1 MACROS THE FRAMEWORK USES

items.title: MODULE-IDENTITY
items.text: Conveys the semantics of an information module.

items.title: OBJECT-TYPE
items.text: Conveys the syntax and semantics of a managed object.

items.title: NOTIFICATION-TYPE
items.text: Conveys the syntax and semantics of a notification.

items.title: TEXTUAL-CONVENTION
items.text: Conveys the syntax and semantics of a new named type.

items.title: MODULE-COMPLIANCE
items.text: Conveys the requirements an agent must meet.

items.title: AGENT-CAPABILITIES
items.text: Conveys the capabilities an agent may offer.

items.title: OBJECT-GROUP
items.text: Groups related objects into one unit of conformance.
